THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Early Art & First Settlements of Africa and the Middle East (to 100 BCE)

Symbolic rock art and sedentary human architecture co-evolved across Africa and Southwest Asia long before conventional classical histories begin. This synthesis tracks the full dual arc through 100 BCE: Pleistocene cave and cliff art from Blombos to Qurta alongside early stone-built villages, temples, Sahara cattle sanctuaries, Dilmun seaports, early West and East African metallurgy centers and Phoenician-Amazigh harbors.

Synthesizes 65 newly expanded Africa & Middle East records alongside the broader Holocene–Pleistocene world catalogue through 100 BCE.

In Toto Specimen Archive · Visual records from caves to open overhangs

Filter verified open-licensed field photographs across traditions, media, and settings—from deep Paleolithic painted caverns like Lascaux and Chauvet to high-desert Nevada overhangs, Saharan canyons, Southern African shelters, and early stone settlements. Dates on rock art are approximate envelopes established by stratigraphy, luminescence, tufa carbonate, or pigment AMS analysis.

Before Agriculture: Late Pleistocene Art & Sedentary Hamlets

Rock art in Africa and Southwest Asia extends deep into the Pleistocene—from geometric engraved ochre at Blombos (~73 ka) and painted stone plaques at Apollo 11 (~27 ka) to the OSL-dated naturalistic aurochs panels overlooking the Upper Egyptian Nile at Qurta (>15 ka) and Antalya cave engravings at Öküzini. By 12,500–9600 BCE, Natufian communities at Ain Mallaha and Epipaleolithic Villagers at Abu Hureyra built circular stone-founded hamlets before full cereal domestication. [1] [5]

Neolithic Sanctuaries, Green Sahara Galleries & Bronze Age Worlds

Across the Early and Middle Holocene, stone sanctuaries at Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe, ʿAin Ghazal's plaster statues, Çatalhöyük's domestic wall murals, and Arabia's life-sized Camel Site sculptures coincided with the wet African Humid Period that turned Tassili n'Ajjer, Tadrart Acacus, Wadi Sura and Niger's Dabous into fertile grazing savannas. By the Bronze and Early Iron Ages, urban archives at Ebla, Mari, Susa and Dilmun stood contemporary with Kushite Kawa/Musawwarat, Eritrean Ona stone towns, Mauritanian Dhar Oualata and Akjoujt copper mines, Nigerian Nok terracotta-and-iron furnaces, Buhaya steel smelters and Punic harbors through 100 BCE. [2] [3] [4] [6] [7] [10] [11]

Timeline Density Through 100 BCE

Every added habitation site (`amea-hab-*`) closes cleanly at or before 100 BCE (or marks clear pre-100 BCE primary layers), while rock-art traditions extending through the second millennium retain their documented multi-period span. [8] [9]

  • Marks on Stone: Global Wall & Rock Art in Toto — Comparative illustrated archive across every inhabited continent—from monumental Paleolithic caves like Lascaux and Sulawesi to desert rock overhangs in Nevada, the Sahara, Australia and Patagonia.
  • Pictographs, Petroglyphs & Painted Caves of North America — Continental survey linking >70 North American rock-art complexes—from Winnemucca Lake and Nevada desert overhangs to Lower Pecos murals, Canadian Shield cliffs and Eastern dark-zone caves—to their Indigenous cultures.
  • Göbekli Tepe, Çatalhöyük & Hattusha — Follow the Anatolian arc from tenth-millennium BCE T-pillar enclosures at Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe to Çatalhöyük’s mudbrick town and Hittite capital Hattusha.
  • Uruk, Ur, Babylon & Nineveh — Trace Mesopotamia’s urban core from Eridu and Uruk’s proto-cuneiform temples through Ur’s Royal Cemetery, Hammurabi’s Babylon and Nineveh’s Assyrian libraries.
  • Saudi Arabia & the Arabian Peninsula (1000 BCE–1900 CE): Incense Oases, Nabataeans, Caliphates & Diriyah — Systematic regional synthesis of Arabian history across three millennia: Taymāʾ and Dadān, Maʾrib and Sabaʾ, Qaryat al-Fāw, Nabataean Hegra, Himyarite Ḥimā, Abbasid Darb Zubaydah, Al-Aḥsāʾ, Historic Jeddah, Oman, and Diriyah/Riyadh.
